extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, scientists and advanced students reflecting on the nature of scientific method and mathematical foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for judging the origin, evidence, and status of axioms, definitions, and deductive sciences — i.e., how to evaluate whether principles or mathematical propositions are empirical, a priori, or hypothetical. Useful for methodological analysis of scientific theories and mathematical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms as experimental inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms (the first principles) are a class of inductions from experience; they rest upon superabundant and obvious evidence and are the simplest and easiest cases of generalization from the facts furnished by our senses or internal consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat axioms as empirical generalizations unless positive argument is given to the contrary. The burden of proof lies with anyone asserting that axioms have a non-experimental (a priori) origin. Example discussion: Poincaré rebuts views that call axioms self-evident independent of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions as provisional/generalizing fictions
rubrics_metrics.description: What are commonly called 'definitions' in demonstrative sciences are generalizations from experience that assert some properties and (for convenience) deny others — a fiction made to exclude modifying circumstances when they are negligible or to defer them when important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating definitions, note they are adopted to simplify inquiry by excluding secondary modifiers; check whether excluded modifiers are indeed negligible in the present inquiry. Example: geometrical 'definitions' presuppose existence of figures meeting the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive (demonstrative) sciences are hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive sciences proceed by tracing consequences of certain assumptions (axioms/definitions) and are therefore hypothetical; their conclusions are true conditional on those suppositions, which may be only approximations to truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) deriving consequences from given hypotheses and (b) establishing the truth/adequacy of the hypotheses themselves. Evaluate both: logical derivation correctness and empirical adequacy of premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate the task of deriving consequences from testing assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative science should perform once-for-all derivations of what follows from assumptions, leaving separate observational or case-specific work to assess how closely the assumptions approximate truth in each instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, 'do all beforehand that can be so done' (i.e., deduce consequences), and reserve empirical testing to determine applicability and the degree of approximation of premises for each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for claims of non-experimental origins
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof lies with those who assert that axioms or first principles are not derived from experience (i.e., are not empirical), and they must supply arguments to that effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand explicit argumentation if anyone claims a principle is a priori; absent such argument, treat the principle as empirically grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability is a psychological/historical phenomenon, not proof of impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent inconceivableness of the negation of an established scientific truth often results from habitual association formed by historical progress of thought; therefore inconceivableness does not prove a proposition impossible or non-experiential in origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating 'inconceivableness' as independent evidence of truth. Use historical examples (e.g., Copernican resistance, Newtonian optics, laws of motion, chemical definite proportions) to show that what becomes inconceivable typically acquired that character through repeated confirmation and mental habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit and association produce the feeling of necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a theory has been long established and the scientific mind forms the habit of conceiving phenomena according to it, other representations disappear from the mental picture and the accepted view comes to seem self-evident or necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that perceived necessity can be an epistemic byproduct of cognitive habituation; when assessing claims of necessity, look for historical and experiential origins rather than relying on subjective feelings of self-evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra/arithmetic are not merely verbal manipulations — each step is an induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Although algebraic symbols may conceal particular images, each step in arithmetic or algebra embodies a real inference from facts to facts; symbols represent 'things in general' but the probative force derives from interpreting symbols as standing for things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept nominalist claims (that numerical propositions are mere definitions or verbal substitutions) without checking the underlying inductive content; in algebra, ensure each symbolic manipulation corresponds to legitimate inference about quantities or numbers of things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty is limited to pure number and unit-equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty (unconditional truth and perfect accuracy) applies only to propositions about pure number, and only so long as numbers are used strictly as counts of identical units; when numbers are applied to real quantities, an implicit assumption (e.g., '1=1' in the relevant respect) is required and may be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying arithmetic/geometry to physical quantities, check the implicit assumption that the units or elements compared are equivalent in the relevant respects (e.g., troy vs avoirdupois pounds, horses of different strength). If units differ, arithmetic conclusions become hypothetical or approximate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of numbers presuppose existence of aggregations (definitions in geometrical sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions like 'Three is two and one' can be regarded as definitions in a geometrical sense but presuppose the existence of collections (aggregations) that exhibit the required arrangements; thus numeric 'definitions' rest on inductive facts about possible configurations of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In teaching or evaluating numerical claims, include sensory/empirical grounding (e.g., using physical objects) to ensure the student or argument is tracking the inductive basis rather than mere symbolic manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of inferences must be assessed when extending number to quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic conclusions are exact when concerning pure number alone, but when number is used as an index to other quantities (weight, strength, time), additional hypotheses about unit equality are required; failing to assess this makes mathematical reasoning hypothetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before inferring non-numerical properties from numerical equality, verify that the units or contexts make such inference legitimate; treat inferences as conditional on quality-equivalence assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution about hypothetical elements in supposedly absolute sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in arithmetic and geometry there may be hypothetical elements: many demonstrative results are only certain given specified approximations in the premises; the peculiar certainty attributed to these sciences often arises from treating approximations as exact for purposes of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging claims of certainty in any demonstrative science, ask which assumptions are approximations and how their inexactness affects conclusions. Be explicit about the margin or kind of approximation tolerated.
